About the Editor

Raphael Dascalu is a native of Sydney, Australia. He completed his BA in Classical Hebrew, Philosophy, and Religious Studies at the University of Sydney (2004); his MA in Comparative Religion at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem (2011); and his PhD in History of Judaism at the University of Chicago (2016). His research is focused primarily on medieval Jewish philosophy in the Islamic world. He currently lives in Melbourne, Australia, and is an Adjunct Research Associate at Monash University.

Editor's Introduction
About Israel b. Samuel al-Maghribī

The works of Israel b. Samuel ha-Dayyan al-Maghribī (Hebrew: ha-Maʿaravi) presented in this publication had a significant impact on Karaite Jewish life from the medieval period into the twentieth century. Despite this, little is known about his own life. We do know that he resided in Cairo, where he served as a dayyan (judge) for the local Karaite community. He is an important source for how Karaite Jews living near the land of Israel endeavored to set the date of the New Year by sending emissaries from their communities to Israel to inspect the state of the barley. Al-Maghribī also wrote a Hebrew poem for the Sabbath, in which he defended the traditional medieval Karaite interpretation that all fire is forbidden on the Sabbath, even if kindled prior to the Sabbath: “If you see me sitting in the dark on the eve of the Sabbath, do not think I am in distress, for God is my light in the darkness.” He appears to have had important and influential disciples, such as Yefet b. Ṣaghīr/Tsaʿir, who authored a Book of Precepts. Al-Maghribī died sometime before 1354.
content.comments:
[1] The Judaeo-Arabic text appears to be corrupt here. The original may have read: …an yaʿtaqida anna -llāha l-ʿālim bi-asrihi. The Arabic version may reflect an emendation of the corrupt text. Our translation reflects the tentative emendation. Cf. Halkin, “A Karaite Creed,” 148: “that He possesses the total universe, the heavens and what is in them…”

[2] This may be a reference to Exodus 15:26, in which God promises to protect the Israelites from the diseases (ha-maḥalah) inflicted upon the Israelites, although the Arabic is ambiguous. Cf. Halkin, “A Karaite Creed,” 150 n. 18.

[3] The term qibla means “direction” and refers to the direction properly faced during prayer (and, according to our author, other devotional acts). There is no accurate English translation that comfortably fits this context.

[4] This translation follows our edition, based on MSS JTSb and BL, which read al-mīʿād (from the root w-ʿ-d). JTSa and BLb read al-maʿād (the Return; from the root ʿ-w-d). Both expressions are widely attested in medieval Arabic literature across schools and genres.

[5] The sense here seems to be that divine judgment takes into account the full range of hidden merit and guilt; according to this reading, connecting the lexeme to the following phrase, it could be read khāfiya. So reads the Arabic version. Alternatively, one could connect the term to the preceding phrase: jumlatan kāfiyatan, “altogether, sufficiently (i.e., fully).” Cf. Halkin, “A Karaite Creed,” 153: “entirely and summarily.” The two possible readings rest on a single diacritic, which is rarely provided in the MSS.

content.english: About the Present Volume

This publication presents the first complete critical edition of both al-Maghribī's theological creed and his short monograph of the laws of ritual slaughter, respectively entitled Al-ʿAqāʾid al-Sitta (The Six Principles) and Shurūṭ al-Dhibāḥa/Dhabīḥa (The Regulations of Slaughter). They are presented in their original Judaeo-Arabic, much as they were transmitted in the Karaite community for centuries. The influence that these works had on Karaite life over that long period is attested in the extent of their distribution. There are several extant manuscripts of the Judaeo-Arabic creed and laws of ritual slaughter, pointing to their continuous use in Karaite study and practice. In the modern period, versions of both the theological creed and the laws of ritual slaughter were published in an Arabic-script version for the benefit of the Egyptian Karaite community. Despite being largely overshadowed by an alternative tradition of ten articles of faith (formalized by Judah Hadassi, twelfth century), al-Maghribī's creed formed the basis for the theological section of a modern Karaite manual. In addition, the Hebrew version of the laws of ritual slaughter survives in a great many manuscripts and has been published at least twice in the modern period.
content.comments:
[6] In its Biblical context, “eternal God” would be a better translation. Our translation of al-Maghribī's usage here more closely reflects Maimonides' understanding of this verse. The latter's usage of this citation as a preface for his works echoes the Islamic basmala (pace Joseph Qafiḥ, for whose discussion see Moreh ha-nebukhim [Mossad Harav Kook: 1977], 3 n. 4). Qafiḥ notes that in employing this formulation, Maimonides expresses his identification with Abraham, the messenger of monotheism in an idolatrous world. In the period following Maimonides, this became a very standard opening in medieval Hebrew and Judaeo-Arabic works. For Maimonides' usage and interpretation of this verse, see Guide of the Perplexed (trans. Shlomo Pines; Chicago: 1963), 3 and n. 1 (introductory epistle), 282 and n. 4 (II.13), 516 (III.29); and cf. Mishneh Torah, Laws of Idolatry and Gentile Norms, 1:3. Saul Lieberman noted that Maimonides prefaces all of his works with this formulation (see Hilkhoth Ha-Yerushalmi (The Laws of the Palestinian Talmud) of Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, ed. Saul Lieberman [The Jewish Theological Seminary of America: 1995], 5, n. 7). Of course, the fact that Maimonides' usage of Gen. 21:33 echoes the basmala does not in the least negate Qafiḥ's insightful observation concerning the significance of this usage.

[7] The term baṣīr may denote either mental insight or physical sight.

[8] It seems that the version attested in JTSb and BLb reflects an erroneous reading of thikhan (without diacritic: תכן) as takūn (תכון).

[9] Despite the fact that JTSb presents the more difficult reading (lectio difficilior) and appears to be older, we have based our text and translation on the version that appears in BL and BLb. The reading sāʾiran wa-jāʾi (sic) is more plausible on two grounds: The formulation is used elsewhere by the same author (see the second tenet of al-Maghribī's creed); and it is arguably cognate with the rabbinic terms holakhah and habaʾah, for which cf. Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Ritual Slaughter, 3:11. This Hebrew terminology is also reflected in Hebrew Karaite works, both medieval and modern: Cf. the formulations ve-yolikh ve-yavi ʿad she-yashlim ha-sheḥiṭah and ve-yolikh ve-yavi ha-sakkin in the eighth chapter of the Hebrew version of al-Maghribī's monograph; Aaron b. Elijah of Nicomedia (fourteenth century), Gan ʿEden, ed. Judah b. Isaac Savuskan (Gözlöw [Eupatoria]: 1864), Ritual Slaughter, 89; and Shemuel Ha-kohen, ʿInyan ha-sheḥiṭah/Ritual Slaughter: A Modern Guide to Karaite Jewish Practice (The Karaite Jews of America: 2017 [republished from 1958 edition]), 18. Cf. Nemoy, “Israel Al-Maghribī's Tract,” 200: “back and forth.” (Nemoy follows the modern Arabic version.)

[10] Reading the Judaeo-Arabic jāra with the Arabic version as jarra, and understanding the term כ̇נק as a variant of the makhnaq (throat). Although ʿunq (as in the Arabic version) is a more common term, (a) the Judaeo-Arabic provides the lectio difficilior, and (b) the term ʿunq refers either to the neck as a whole or to the nape or back of the neck, which makes less sense in this context.

content.english: In order to present a more complete picture of al-Maghribī's impact on Karaite Jewish life, we have included as appendices the version of al-Maghribī's aforementioned works as they were published in Arabic script in Egypt in the early twentieth century, and the Hebrew version of the laws of slaughter, which differs significantly from the (Judaeo-)Arabic versions. The latter circulated widely, as attested by the many manuscripts in which it survives. A detailed comparison of the various versions of al-Maghribī's works is beyond the scope of the present volume, as is the production of a critical edition of the Hebrew laws of slaughter. These remain a desideratum.
content.comments: [11] Cf. Nemoy, “Israel Al-Maghribi's Tract,” 201.

content.english: A Note on the Linguistic and Cultural Context of these Works

Our author lived and produced his writings in the Islamic world, in an Arabic-speaking milieu. Unlike the Jews of the Latin West in this period, educated Jews in the Islamic world tended to be deeply and openly engaged in the dominant intellectual cultures of their society. Both Karaite and Rabbanite Jews adopted Arabic literary models, as well as theological, philosophical, and scientific terminology. These became thoroughly integrated into Jewish literature. Like many Karaite and Rabbanite writers before him, al-Maghribī wrote in Judaeo-Arabic, which is to say, Arabic written in Hebrew script and selectively employing Hebrew or Aramaic terms and phrases (code-switching). Like other writers in this cultural context, he regularly employs Arabic names for God (e.g., Allāh) and pious formulas (e.g., tabāraka wa-taʿālā, “may He be blessed and exalted!”). He also assumes familiarity with the common Arabic terminology of Jewish and Muslim texts in the Islamic world. It should thus not be surprising to see that he employs such terms as qibla (the direction of prayer) or the Qurʾanic formulation al-ḥamd li-ʾllāhrabb al-ʿālamīn (“praise to God, Master of Worlds”). Such expressions had long been assimilated into Jewish literature within the Islamic world.
Editor's Introduction to the Six Principles of Faith: al-Maghribī's Theological Creed

What makes al-Maghribī's creed unique is its popular character. Composed in Judaeo-Arabic, it is simple, elegant, and brief—and most likely intended as an educational tool for instruction in Karaite Judaism, a catechism of sorts. Al-Maghribī's creed is notably free of any overt commitment to a theological or philosophical school of thought, preferring instead to articulate the fundamental tenets of faith in their broadest terms. The themes explored by al-Maghribī in his creed are as follows: (i) belief in God (including some treatment of attributes), (ii) belief in the messengership of Moses, (iii) belief in the prophets in general, (iv) belief in the Torah, (v) affirmation of the holy site (qibla, lit. “direction” [i.e., of prayer]), and (vi) belief in the Day of Judgment. Although there is some overlap with the structure of the Islamic creed, al-Maghribī does not appear to have constrained himself to earlier literary models.
content.comments:
[12] The Judaeo-Arabic version attested in JTSb and BL appears to be corrupt here, due to a series of scribal errors and emendations (apparently wṣyd > wṣyr > yṣyr > wyṣyr [wa-yaṣīr]; both yod/vav and dalet/resh are easily confused in Hebrew script). Our edition and translation follow BLb and the Arabic-script version, providing the variants in the critical apparatus.

[13] The Judaeo-Arabic text in JTSb and BL is corrupt here and difficult to decipher. On purely textual grounds, our text follows JTSb and BL, presenting as they do the lectio difficilior. Our translation follows BLb, despite the fact that it presents the lectio facilior, as it is at least decipherable.

content.english: In the third tenet, the miracles (muʿjizāt) of the prophets are emphasized, a theme that features prominently in Islamic prophetology. His assertion of the reliability of prophetic accounts, and his defense of the continuity of prophetic traditions, appears to be motivated by polemical concerns—namely, as a retort to the Muslim accusation of taḥrīf (corruption of Scripture). The same concern likely motivates the forceful assertion of the accuracy and perfection of the Torah, appearing in the fourth tenet. Al-Maghribī's emphasis on Moses' role as the revealer of the Law, with other prophets merely modeling and affirming the Torah of Moses while innovating nothing, likely reflects his post-Maimonidean context.
content.comments:
[15] Compare Targum Onqelos, and Ibn Ezra's interpretation ad loc.; this also reflects al-Maghribī's interpretation of shehiyyah as a response to being startled.

[16] Compare Ibn Ezra's commentary ad loc., where he explains לא גרמו as לא שברו עצם (cf. Aramaic g-r-m as “bone”).

[17] Apparently identifying the root ḥ-l-d as a metathesis of ḥ-d-l; compare Ibn Ezra ad loc.

content.english: In Islamic tradition, Jerusalem is called “the first of the two qiblas” (ūlā al-qiblatayn), occupying its status before being replaced by Mecca. Al-Maghribī's argument in the fifth tenet for the centrality of Jerusalem as the eternal qibla, the locus toward which prayer and other ritual acts should be directed, may thus be understood as a response to Muslim practice. The author further emphasizes that all the nations of the earth will ultimately turn to Jerusalem in worship.
content.comments: [18] All of the Judaeo-Arabic manuscripts available to us seem to read ʿadiya. The text appears to be corrupt, possibly reflecting a scribal error ʿariya > ʿadiya. The Arabic version (ʿudda), apart from remaining difficult to understand, seems to reflect an interpretation of the latter reading. The translation follows the suggested emendation.

content.english: In the sixth and final tenet of al-Maghribī's creed, a striking element is the author's insistence on the eternal punishment of the wicked. Although this is not the dominant attitude in rabbinic sources, it does reflect a widespread consensus among Karaite thinkers. It is also, of course, consistent with both Christian and Muslim attitudes.
content.comments: [19] This section bears no title in the original Judaeo-Arabic; we have added one to assist the reader's transition to this new topic. Please note that our translations of animal anatomy are tentative.

content.english: Al-Maghribī's creed provides us with a window not only into the worldview of a Karaite Jewish scholar of the fourteenth century, but into the intellectual and spiritual life of the community as a whole over an extended period. This may be said on account of the continuous copying and publication of the creed over the centuries, and in particular due to its catechismal quality. In the absence of direct evidence, one can only imagine generations of Karaite children and laypersons being taught this creed as their introduction to the theological principles of their ancestral faith—and while this certainly remains a matter of conjecture, it is also an eminently plausible interpretation of the work and its purpose.
Editor's Introduction to al-Maghribī's Treatise on Ritual Slaughter

Al-Maghribī's explicit and otherwise surprising mention of ritual slaughter in the fourth tenet of his creed (regarding the belief in the Torah) suggests that the two works were originally written in close succession and intended to be studied or at least distributed together. The same theme (viz., gratitude to God for permitting the slaughter and consumption of animals) is raised explicitly in the ninth chapter of the laws of slaughter, in connection with reciting the benediction.

This work consists of ten chapters on the laws of slaughter, followed by three addenda that appear in the extant manuscripts. Among the particularly notable positions taken in this work by the author are that the slaughterer must believe in the theory of compensation, a view rejected by later Karaite authorities (Chapter I); that the animal may not be pregnant, a law followed by Karaites to this day (Chapter II); that the slaughterer should face Jerusalem during the slaughter (Chapter VIII); and that the blessing recited over the act of slaughter reflects the Karaite theological conception, repeated in this work and the creed, that God permitted human beings to slaughter animals for consumption (Chapter IX).
content.comments: [20] The Judaeo-Arabic version appears to be corrupt here. JTSb, BLb, and the Arabic version have מכ̇צה / مخصة without a diacritic over the ṣād, while BL reads מכ̇צ̇ה. (It should be noted, however, that BLb is extremely inconsistent in applying diacritics, even in cases where this is common in Judaeo-Arabic MSS, e.g., to indicate ḍād and ẓāʾ.) The former reading makes little sense, and the most plausible (though still awkward, and certainly speculative) emendation would have מכ̇צצה̈. If BL does not reflect the original version, the copyist of BL (or the copyist of the vorlage) may have emended the ṣād to a ḍād in an attempt to read the lexeme as a specific anatomical term, derived from the root m-kh-ḍ (to shake or churn [e.g., milk]). This could plausibly refer to the mammary artery.

content.english: The three addenda concern (i) the factors that invalidate slaughter, (ii) the belief in compensation for the slaughtered animal, and (iii) the parts of the animal to be removed after slaughter.

The first of these addenda, on the factors that invalidate slaughter, is particularly striking in the way that it attempts to balance an openness to Rabbanite practice with an assertion of Karaite independence. Jacob al-Qirqisānī, a highly influential Karaite scholar of the tenth century, explicitly criticized the Rabbanites for their adherence to a list of five factors that invalidate slaughter:

[The Rabbanites forbid] what God Himself has not forbidden, and of which no mention is to be found, such as ... the conditions for slaughtering which they list in the rules of slaughtering, viz. delay, pressure, digging, slipping, and tearing. They contradict completely: `Thou shalt not add [thereto], nor diminish from it'.

Al-Maghribī, on the other hand, accepts the terms of the rabbinic sources but insists on the primacy of independent analysis (naẓar) in defining them. He therefore cites proof texts for their usage. This adds a scripturalist hue to an otherwise very rabbinic-sounding passage. It may be that Karaite communities had already adopted such a position. Alternatively, al-Maghribī may simply be acknowledging that in the absence of further detail, extra-Biblical tradition is helpful, and in this case does not contradict the Biblical text.

It should be noted that contemporary Karaite communities of Egyptian descent accept neither al-Maghribī's list of five factors nor al-Qirqisānī's rejection of them. Instead, they identify ten disqualifying factors, integrating and expanding the earlier enumeration.

In his second addendum, the Chapter on the Principles of Judgment [After Death], al-Maghribī raises the theme of divine justice, which is directly opposed to injustice. Futility or waste (ʿabath) is considered to be a variety of evil or repugnance (qubḥ/al-qabīḥ) and must therefore not be attributed to God. But if this is the case, how is it that the Divine permitted human beings to harm animals? Here, al-Maghribī discusses four possible factors that may justify harm in general and determines that only one of them can conceivably justify the slaughter of animals: namely, that God will provide the animal with recompense in the Hereafter (it is not necessary for us to know precisely what kind of recompense). This concern with divine justice or theodicy, and more specifically the terminology used in this case, are typical of the Muʿtazilite school of Islamic systematic theology (kalām), which had contributed considerably to Karaite and Rabbanite thought over the preceding centuries.

The final addendum discusses the parts of the animal that must be removed following slaughter. It is interesting to note that many Karaites today continue to remove the sciatic nerve (gid ha-nasheh) in birds, a practice that matches the Judaeo-Arabic version of al-Maghribī's monograph but is left undetermined in the widely circulated Hebrew version. The removal of the gid ha-nasheh from birds is already attested to in the writings of al-Qirqisānī, who preceded al-Maghribī by some four centuries. The continuation of this practice into the present demonstrates the continued influence of works such as al-Maghribī's (even if not his precise work). This is supported by the fact that the Hebrew manual on ritual slaughter used by the Egyptian Karaite community of the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries specifically states that the prohibition does not apply to birds. We thus return to our point that Karaite communal and religious life has been shaped by a variety of literature, among which al-Maghribī's works have occupied a prominent place.
About the Judaeo-Arabic Edition and English Translation
The Judaeo-Arabic text is based on four manuscripts:

1. JTS MS 3434/Adler 202 (JTSa): Written in a semi-cursive Oriental hand, of uncertain date. This MS contains most of the text of al-Maghribī's creed. It is missing at least two leaves, including a significant portion of the first of al-Maghribī's theological principles (Arabic: ʿaqāʾid, sing. ʿaqīda), and part of the concluding principle. It differs from the other two manuscripts in many of its readings and represents a distinct manuscript tradition.

2. JTS MS 3436/Adler 249 (JTSb): Written in a semi-cursive Oriental hand, of uncertain date. This MS contains the creed and laws of slaughter (including the handling of animals, laws pertaining to the relevant blessings, etc.). The first two leaves are badly damaged and furnish a very limited part of the text that they originally contained.

3. British Library Oriental Manuscript 2528 (BL): This is the first of two manuscripts catalogued together. According to the colophon, it was completed by Joseph b. Abraham Levi on Monday, 23rd of Kislev, 5592 AM (28th of November, 1831 CE). It is written in a clear semi-cursive Oriental script. This manuscript bears a very close affinity with the much older JTS 3436 (JTSb), but seems not to have been copied from it.

4. British Library Oriental Manuscript 2528 (BLb): The second of the two manuscripts catalogued together is missing the opening leaf of the creed, while the first extant leaf is somewhat damaged. It is of uncertain dating and bears some affinity with JTS 3434 (JTSa). Like the other manuscripts, it is in a semi-cursive Oriental script. It should be noted that despite otherwise not resembling BL, it shares one ornamental feature with that manuscript—namely, a broken “roof” (similar to the Rabbanite ḥaṭoṭeret) on some letters, particularly when lengthened for aesthetic reasons. Some of the Hebrew verses and blessings are vocalized, and the irregularities of the vocalization (e.g., confusion of qamets and pataḥ) point to the copyist's Palestinian (“Sephardic”) pronunciation. This is of some interest, as the Babylonian pronunciation is widely attested in manuscripts from Egypt and the Levant into the late medieval period. Catalogued together with the two manuscripts of al-Maghribī's creed and laws of ritual slaughter are several fragments of a much longer work dealing with legal and theological aspects of ritual slaughter, which may or may not be authored by al-Maghribī (although there are certainly common concerns and terminology between the works). This work is in a different hand, in a beautiful semi-cursive Oriental script. Due to its fragmentary nature and uncertain provenance, the work has not been included in the present volume.

Due to the condition of the manuscripts, the edition presented here is neither purely diplomatic (i.e., based on a single manuscript with variants noted) nor eclectic (i.e., an attempt at reconstructing an original text from the various manuscripts, where the final version may differ significantly from any single extant manuscript). Rather, due to the very close affinity between JTSb and BL and their relative completeness, we have decided to base the body of the text on that manuscript tradition. In the absence of other considerations, we have preferred JTSb when the two manuscripts differ. Where any manuscript provides an orthography that is closer to standard literary Arabic, that orthography has been selected for the body of the text. Where all versions of the Judaeo-Arabic differ significantly from standard literary Arabic, even in cases where this might be more straightforwardly construed as an error, we have retained the form in the MSS. All variants are noted. Abbreviations in the manuscripts are presented in full in the body of the edition, but are retained in the variants.

Regarding diacritics, the Judaeo-Arabic orthography has been standardized to follow near-universal practice in published Judaeo-Arabic works; however, the original orthography of the manuscripts has been retained in the variants. To aid in identifying Biblical citations, verses are rendered in a different typeset that includes cantillation marks, followed by the Biblical reference in superscript. Square brackets [abc] in the Judaeo-Arabic text indicate a questionable reading (e.g., in cases of limited legibility); rounded parentheses (abc) indicate alternative readings, explained in the critical apparatus; arrowhead brackets <abc> indicate passages that appear in some versions of the text, while being omitted from others.

In general, the English translation reflects the body of the Judaeo-Arabic text as presented in the present edition. In the few cases in which we have relied on the reading or interpretation reflected in the Arabic edition, or on a suggested emendation, this is noted. Since the introduction covers the most significant themes that arise in the text and explores the work's broader context, the notes to the text generally focus on narrowly textual concerns and problems of translation. Glosses or interpolations for the sake of clarity in English appear in square brackets. Biblical citations are largely based on the JPS Tanakh (2003), with emendations based on their use in context and medieval interpretive traditions.

Appendices
Introduction to Appendices

As noted in the introduction, in order to present a more complete picture of the lasting impact of al-Maghribī's works on the Karaite Jewish community, we have republished the following editions as appendices:

content.hebrew: בְּשֵׁם ייי נַעֲשֶׂה וְנַצְלִיחַ
content.english: In the name of the Lord, let us act and prevail.

content.hebrew: נבתדי אלאן בתרתיב אלעקאיד אלסתה̈ אלד̇י לְמָרֵינוּ וְרַבֵּינוּ נִזְרֵינוּ וְכִתְרֵינוּ וַעֲטֶרֶת רֹאשֵׁינוּ וּצְנִיף תִּפְאַרְתֵּינוּ הוֹדֵנוּ וַהֲדָרֵנוּ הֶחָכָם הַמּוּפְלֶה אֲשֶׁר הוּא לְסוֹדוֹת וַעֲמוּקּוֹת מְגַלֶּה כְּבוֹד הָרַב יִשְׂרָאֵל הַדַּיָּן בֶּן כְּבוֹד גְּדֻלָּתוֹ וּקְדֻשָּׁתוֹ אֲשֶׁר שָׂם הַחָכְמָה אוֹמַנְתּוֹ וְהַבִּינָה מֵנִקְתּוֹ הַגְּבִיר הַנִּכְבָּד בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מָרֵינוּ וְרַבֵּינוּ שְׁמוּאֵל הַמַּעֲרָבִי תְּהִי נַפְשׁוֹ צְרוּרָ֣ה ׀ בִּצְר֣וֹר הַחַיִּ֗ים ((שְׁמוּאֵל א כה׃כט)) אָמֵן נֶצַח סֶלָה וְשָׁלוֹם עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל׃
content.english: Here begins the order of the six principles of faith, by our master and teacher, our diadem, our crowning garland, our glorious adorning headdress, our magnificence, the distinguished sage, revealer of secrets and profundities, the honorable R. Israel the Judge (ha-dayyan), son of the honorable, great and saintly one who appointed Wisdom and Discernment as his nurse, noble and honored in Israel, our master and teacher Samuel the Judge (ha-dayyan) ha-Maʿaravi, may his soul be bound up in the bond of life (1 Samuel 25:29). Amen, Neṣaḥ, Selah; and peace upon all Israel.

content.hebrew: אלעקידה̈ אלאולה
content.english: The First Tenet

content.hebrew:
אעתקאד אלרבוביה̈

יג̇ב עלי כל בַּר יִשְׂרָאֵל אן יעתקד אן לה אלעאלם באסרה והו אלסמא ומא פיהא ואלארץ̇ ומא עליהא ואלבחאר ומא יאויהא ואלג̇באל ואואדיהא כ̇אלק ואחד ג̇ל ג̇לאלה לא אול לה ולא אכ̇ר לא גאלב לה ולא קאהר לא פוק לה פיכ̇פצ̇ה ולא תחת לה פירפעה ולא ג̇ואנב לה פתשד̇ה ולא ג̇האת לה פיתחדה אראד אן יכון מא שא פכאן ואחדתה פי לא זמאן ולא מכאן ואוג̇ד אלמוג̇ודאת מן אלעדם ואתפרד מן דונהם באלקדם ואנה חי לא ימות באקי לא יפנא גניא לא יפתקר ג̇ואד לא יבכ̇ל חכים לא יג̇הל אחאט עלמה בכל אלמעלומאת אלמאצ̇י ואלחאצ̇ר ומא הו את כל אלמוג̇ודאת מפתקרה̈ אליה ואעתמאדהא פי כפאיתהא עליה לא יתכת̇ר בתכת̇יר צפאתה ולא יזאד ולא ינקץ פי ד̇אתה לא ידרך באלחואס אלכ̇מס ותעלי ען אלד̇וק ואללמס לא יקאל ענה אנה ערץ̇ ולא ג̇והר ולא יכ̇פא ללחס ויט̇הר ולא אנה ינאם ויסהר ולא אנה יגלב ויוקהר ולא הו ג̇סם ולא קוה̈ פי ג̇סם אסמה אללה מא אעזה מן אסם לא תנפעה אלטאעה̈ ולא תצ̇רה אלמעציה̈ סמיע אלדעואת קאבל אלתובאת מקל אלעת̇ראת מפרג̇ אלכרבאת מנג̇י מן אלאפאת גפר אלזלאת צאדק אלועד חאפט̇ אלעהד חנאן מנאן צולטאן דיאן ארחם אלראחמין אכ̇ד̇ חק אלמט̇לומין מן אלט̇אלמין מעווץ̇ אלצאברין ואלמאלומין אחכאמה לא ג̇ור פיהא ואואמרה ונואהיה לא פסאד יעתריהא והו אלממית אלמחיי אלממרץ̇ אלמשפי אלמפקר אלמגני לא אלאה סואה אלד̇י תסג̇ד לג̇לאל ג̇מאל ג̇לאלה ולכמאל עט̇מתה אלג̇באה ותנטק בתסביחה ותנזיהה אלאפואה לא נעמה̈ גיר נעמאה תבארך ותקדס ותסבח ותמג̇ד ותרפע ותנזה ותבהג̇ עז וג̇ל ותעאלי אסמה אלאעט̇ם לאבד אלאבדין ונסאלה סבחאנה ותעאלי אן יעצמנא מן אלכ̇טא ואלזלל פי אלדניא ואלדין ולא יג̇עלנא מן אלמלחדין אמין אמין ואלחמד ללה רב אלעאלמין׃
content.english:
Belief in Divinity

Every Israelite must believe that God possesses complete knowledge of the heavens and all that is in them, of the earth and all that is upon it, of the seas and their inhabitants, of the mountains and their valleys. Sole Creator, exceedingly majestic, with neither beginning nor end. He can neither be overpowered, nor conquered; He has no upper limit that might set Him below, nor a lower limit that might set Him above; He has no flanks that might contain Him, nor sides that might delimit Him. Whatever He wills to be, comes to be; His Oneness is timeless and placeless; He brought all that exists into being from nothing, timelessly remaining separate from them. He lives and does not die, endures and does not perish; He is self-sufficient and not in need, generous and not miserly, wise and not ignorant. His knowledge encompasses all things past, present, and future. All creatures depend upon Him, and place their trust in His sufficiency. He does not become many with the multiplication of His attributes; He neither grows nor shrinks in His essence; He is imperceptible to the five senses, transcending both taste and touch. Let it not be said that He is an accident or a substance, that He disappears or that He appears to the senses, that He slumbers or that He wakes, that He may be overpowered or conquered, or that He is a body or a power in a body. His name is “God” (allāh); no name is mightier than His. Obedience does not benefit Him, and sin does not harm Him. He hears all prayer, accepts repentance, supports those who stumble, dispels grief, delivers from ruin, forgives sin, is faithful to promises, keeps His covenant; Bestower, Compassionate One, Ruler, Judge, Most Merciful of All; who takes up the claim of the oppressed against the oppressors; who requites the steadfast and those who suffer. There is not a trace of injustice in His judgments; His commandments and prohibitions are untainted by corruption. He puts to death and gives life, brings illness and heals, allots poverty and wealth. There is no god other than Him, His Sublime Highness and Perfect Majesty, to whom all foreheads bow, of whom all mouths speak in praise and exaltation. There is no favor but His favor.

May His most great name be blessed, sanctified, praised, glorified, esteemed, extolled above all else, delighted in, declared mighty and sublime, and exalted forever and ever! We ask Him (may He be praised and exalted) to safeguard us from offense and error in this world, and in [matters of] religion; and let Him not consider us among the unbelievers.

Amen, Amen, and praise be to God, the Lord of Worlds.
content.comments: [1] The Judaeo-Arabic text appears to be corrupt here. The original may have read: …an yaʿtaqida anna -llāha l-ʿālim bi-asrihi. The Arabic version may reflect an emendation of the corrupt text. Our translation reflects the tentative emendation. Cf. Halkin, “A Karaite Creed,” 148: “that He possesses the total universe, the heavens and what is in them…”

content.hebrew: אלעקידה̈ אלת̇אניה̈
content.english: The Second Tenet

content.hebrew:
אעתקאד אלרסלייה̈

הו אן יעתקד אן אכמל נוע אלאנסאני כ̇לקא ועקלא וד̇הנא ותמייזא ושרפא ותואצ̇עא ואג̇לאלא ואכראמא הו אלסייד אלמשרף אלמכרם אלמעט̇ם קדוה̈ אלאנביא ואלמרסלין ואמאם אלאולין ואלאכ̇רין אלד̇י אג̇מעת עלי צחה̈ צדקה ותצדיק רסאלאתה ותת̇בית מעג̇זאתה סאיר אלמליין ושהדו לה בתכלים רב אלעזה̈ ג̇מיע אלנביין ואדעאה רבה לינאג̇יה פי אעלא עליין ואן מן מעג̇זאתה קלב אלעצא ת̇עבאן ורדהא וקלב אליד ביצ̇א ועאודהא ומא צנעה מן אלבראהין ואלאיאת פי אלעשר צ̇רבאת אלמרג̇פאת אלד̇י אדען לה פרעון דפעאת ת̇ם שק בחר אלעג̇אג̇ ואנבע מן אלצכ̇ר מא מתדאפק אלאמואג̇ ואברא מן אלבלוי ועלי ידה אנזל אלמָן ואלסלוי וברפע ידיה הזמת אלג̇באב̇רה̈ ובג̇אהה ד̇לת אלמלוך אלקאהרה̈ כולהם שפאהא עלי ג̇בל אלטור ותלאלא עלי וג̇הה אלכרים מן לדא אלאלאה נור ותסלם מן אלמלא אלאעלא לוחין ג̇והר מכנון פיהום כלאם אללה מסטור שפע פשפע אלעאציין וראי מואכב אלחצ̇רה̈ אלקדוסייה̈ סאירין וג̇איין זאד עלי כאפה̈ אלאנביא פי אלעז ואלשרף כזיאדה̈ אלשמס עלי אלקמר אד̇א אנחרף לאנה בדרהם וצדרהם ועליה ידור אמרהם הו סיידנא וקדותנא ואמאמנא ותאג̇ ראסנא ועמוד כ̇ימתנא ווסילתנא אלי מעבודנא ורב שרענא הו סיידנא מוסי אלכלים אבן עמראן סלאם אללה תעלי עליה ועלי אסלאפה אלכראם סלאמא מרצ̇ייא אלי יום אלדין ואלחמד ללה רב אלעאלמין אמין׃
content.english:
Belief in Messengership

One must believe that the most perfect specimen of humanity with respect to moral dispositions, intellect, mind, judgment, dignity, humility, eminence, and nobility was the illustrious and noble and venerated master; the exemplar of all prophets and messengers, leader of the ancients and moderns, concerning whom all those who profess religion (al-milliyyīn) have concurred, affirming the soundness of his true message, declaring his messages to be true, and upholding his miracles. All of the prophets have testified that he spoke with the Lord Almighty, and that his Lord summoned him, entrusting him into His confidence in the uppermost heavens. Among his miracles: he turned the staff into a snake, and back (Exodus 4:3–4); he turned his hand white, and back (Exodus 4:6–7); the proofs and signs that he produced with the ten quaking plagues, smiting Pharaoh (Exodus 7–12); then he parted the raging sea (Exodus 14:16–28); he brought waves of flowing water forth from the rock (Exodus 17:5–7); he healed affliction; he brought down manna and quail [from the sky] (Exodus 16:1–36); by lifting his hands, he defeated tyrants (Exodus 17:8–13); by his glory, conquering kings were brought low (Numbers 21:21–35); he addressed [the Israelites] on Mount Sinai (cf. Exodus 20:16); his noble face was illuminated with godly light (Exodus 34:29–30); he received two inscribed tablets from the Heavenly Host, containing a hidden jewel, inscribed with the word of God (Exodus 31:18); an intercessor, who interceded on behalf of recalcitrant sinners (Exodus 32:11–14); he watched the processions of the Holy Regent, coming and going. He exceeds all of the other prophets in might and nobility, as the sun outshines the setting moon; for he is their full moon and their commander (badruhum wa-ṣadruhum), their authority revolves around him. He is our master, our exemplar, our leader, the crown of our head, the pillar of our tent, our intercessor before the One whom we worship, possessor of our Law, Moses the Spokesman, the son of Amram (mūsā al-kalīm ibn ʿimrān). May God Most High's peace be upon him, and upon his noble predecessors—gratifying peace until the Day of Judgment.

Praise be to God, the Lord of Worlds, Amen.
content.comments: [2] This may be a reference to Exodus 15:26, in which God promises to protect the Israelites from the diseases (ha-maḥalah) inflicted upon the Israelites, although the Arabic is ambiguous. Cf. Halkin, “A Karaite Creed,” 150 n. 18.

content.hebrew: אלעקידה̈ אלת̇אלת̇ה̈
content.english: The Third Tenet

content.hebrew:
אעתקאד אלנביין ואלמרסלין מן אתא קבלה ומעה ובעדה

הו אן יעתקד אן מן נטקת בה אלכתב אלצאדקה̈ בצחה̈ נבותה כאן ד̇לך מן קבלה כסיידנא אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב אֲבוֹתֵינוּ עֲלֵיהֶם הַשָּׁלוֹם אלמקול ענהם אַֽל־תִּגְּעוּ֙ בִּמְשִׁיחָ֔י וּבִנְבִיאַ֖י אַל־תָּרֵֽעוּ׃ ((דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א טז:כב)) ומן עצרה מת̇ל סיידנא אַהֲרֹן וסיידנא אֶלְעָזָר וסיידנא פִּינְחָס וסיידנא יְהוֹשֻׁעַ ואלשִׁבְעִים זְקֵינִים עֲלֵיהֶם הַשָּׁלוֹם ומן בעדה מת̇ל סיידנא שְׁמוּאֵל הָרָמָתִי וסיידנא אֵלִיָּהוּ וסיידנא אֱלִישָׁע וסיידנא יְשַׁעְיָה וְיִרְמְיָה וִיחֶזְקֵאל וסיידנא דָּנִיֵּאל ורפקאה עֲלֵיהֶם הַשָּׁלוֹם אלד̇י קאמת להם אלמעג̇זאת וג̇את עלי ידהם אלבינאת באלבראהין ואלאיאת נחו וקוף אלשמס ואלקמר לסיידנא יְהוֹשֻׁעַ וארתפאע אלובא באלמַחְתָּה לסיידנא אַהֲרֹן ואמא אלסייד אֵלִיָּהוּ משי בין אלמיאה ונזול אלנאר לה מן אלסמא ואחיא אבן אלצָרְפִית ונזול אלמטר בדעאה וחלול אלברכה̈ למן אצ̇אפה וסיידנא אֱלִישָׁע עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם איצ̇א משי בין אלמיאה ואטלע ראש אלפאס מן אלואד ואחיא אבן אלשׁוּנַמִּית ומא אכ̇תץ בה איצ̇א כל נבי ונבי מנהם מן אלאיאת ואלבראהין ממא שרח ג̇מיעה שייא יטול וצדקהם פיה מנקול לא שך פיה ולא ריב יעת̇ריה ואן כל מנהם בשריעה̈ אֲדוֹנֵינוּ מֹשֶׁה בֶּן עַמְרָם אַב הַנְּבִיאִים מקתדיין ובהא מחקקין ומצדקין ובהא עאלמין ועאמלין ולא יג̇דד עלי יד אחד מנהם לא שרע ולא דין ואלאמאנה̈ בצדקהם מחקקין סלאם אללה תעאלי עליהם אג̇מעין אמין ואלחמד ללה רב אלעאלמין אמין׃
content.english:
Belief in the Prophets and Messengers Who Came Before

[Moses], at the Same Time as He Did, and After Him

This is the belief in those of whose reliable prophecy the True Books speak. This is the case concerning those preceding Moses, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (peace be upon them), concerning whom it has been said, Do not touch My anointed ones; do not harm My prophets (1 Chronicles 16:22). Among his contemporaries were Aaron, Eleazar, Phineas, Joshua, and the seventy elders (peace be upon them). Among those following him were such figures as Samuel the Rama­thite, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel and his companions (peace be upon them). [These are the prophets] for whose sake miracles occurred, and through whom demonstrations, proofs, and signs came to pass, such as the halting of the sun and moon for Joshua (Joshua 10:12), and the elimination of the plague by Aaron, using his fire-pan (Numbers 17:11). Elijah walked between the [parted] waters (2 Kings 2:14), caused fire to descend from heaven (ibid., 1:12), resuscitated the Zarephathite woman's son (1 Kings 17:9,17–24), caused rain to pour from heaven by his supplication (1 Kings 17:1,18:1), and brought blessings upon those who hosted him. Elisha (peace be upon him) also walked between the [parted] waters (2 Kings 2:14), made an axe head float (2 Kings 6:1–7), and resuscitated the Shunammite woman's son (2 Kings 4:8,12,18–37). This includes the signs and proofs that are particular to each and every one of the prophets, a full account of which would be too lengthy. Their truth has been transmitted, unafflicted by doubt or dispute. Each modeled the Law (sharīʿa) of Moses, son of Amram, father of the prophets, fulfilling and affirming it, acquiring knowledge and acting (ʿālimīn wa-ʿāmilīn) in accordance with it. None innovated any new law, religion, or belief; indeed, their sincerity is well established. God's peace be upon them all.

Amen, and praise be to God, the Lord of Worlds, Amen.

content.hebrew: אלעקידה̈ אלראבעה̈
content.english: The Fourth Tenet

content.hebrew:
אעתקאד אלרסאלה̈

הו אן יעתקד אן אלשריעה̈ אלטאהרה̈ אלמקדסה̈ אלמעט̇מה̈ אלמסמאה̈ באלתּוֹרָה יַגְדִּילָהּ וְיַאְדִּירָהּ בִּלְבַב כָּל הַבְּרִיּוֹת כמא בשר אלנבי וקאל יְהֹוָ֥ה חָפֵ֖ץ לְמַ֣עַן צִדְק֑וֹ יַגְדִּ֥יל תּוֹרָ֖ה וְיַאְדִּֽיר׃ ((יְשַׁעְיָהוּ מב׃כא)) והי אלד̇י אמלית עלי יד סיידנא מֹשֶׁה עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אלאמין מן אלמלא אלאעלא בגיר ואסטה̈ כלמה̈ כלמה̈ וחרף חרף מחררה אלחרוף ואלכלאם פציחה̈ צריחה̈ לא תנאקץ̇ פיהא ולא שך יעתריהא חק מחץ̇ שריעה̈ כאמלה̈ ואחכאמהא עאדלה̈ לא תפסך̇ אבדא ולא תבטל סרמדא צח נקלהא בתואתר אלאכ̇באר ות̇בתת צחתהא בתואתר אלאעצאר ואנהא פי כ̇מסה̈ אספאר טאבקת אלעקול מעאניהא פצדקתהא וסמעת סאיר אלמליין אחכאמהא פעט̇מתהא ואד̇נת ען מנזלתהא באבאחה̈ ד̇באחה̈ אלחיואן לשרף חכמה̈ אלמביח ען מא תצ̇מנת חכמתהא אלעקול ואלאד̇האן לעדלה̈ אלמת̇בות פיהא וחכמה̈ אלנאפד̇ עליהא לא יקאיסהא כתאב ולא תעתרצ̇הא ד̇וי אלאלבאב כמא קאל ענהא ג̇ל מן קאל כׇּל־כְּלִ֞י יוּצַ֤ר עָלַ֙יִךְ֙ לֹ֣א יִצְלָ֔ח וְכׇל־לָשׁ֛וֹן תָּקוּם־אִתָּ֥ךְ לַמִּשְׁפָּ֖ט תַּרְשִׁ֑יעִי זֹ֡את נַחֲלַת֩ עַבְדֵ֨י יְהֹוָ֧ה וְצִדְקָתָ֛ם מֵאִתִּ֖י נְאֻם־יְהֹוָֽה׃ ((יְשַׁעְיָהוּ נד׃יז))
content.english:
Belief in the Message

One must believe that the pure, sacred, and sublime Law, which is called the Torah—may God magnify and glorify it in the hearts of all the creatures, as the prophet proclaimed, The Lord desires His [servant's] vindication, that he may magnify and glorify his Torah (Isaiah 42:21)—is that which was dictated to our faithful master Moses (peace be upon him) by the Heavenly Host, without any intermediary: word by word, letter for letter, accurately recording the letters and discourse; eloquent, pure, sullied by neither contradiction nor doubt, sheer truth; a perfect Law, with just decrees; for all eternity, it will never be abrogated nor annulled; its transmission ensured by the unbroken succession of reports, its correctness ensured throughout the ages. It is comprised of five books. Intellects have affirmed their content and deemed them true. All those who profess religion (al-milliyyīn) have heard its decrees and extolled them. From its exalted station, it informed us concerning the permissibility of slaughtering animals, attesting to the noble wisdom of the Permitter, surpassing the wisdom that can be comprehended by intellects and minds in its demonstrable justness, and the wisdom of the One who affects its application. No book is comparable to it; none gifted with an understanding heart can oppose it. As He said (glory be to Him) concerning it, No weapon formed against you shall succeed, and every tongue that contends with you at law you shall defeat. Such is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord, such their triumph through Me—declares the Lord (Isaiah 54:17).

content.hebrew: אלעקידה̈ אלכ̇אמסה̈
content.english: The Fifth Tenet

content.hebrew:
אעתקאד אלקבלה̈

הו אן יעתקד אן אלקבלה̈ אלקדוסייה̈ אלמכרמה̈ אלמעט̇מה̈ אעאדהא אללה תעאלי אלי עזהא ושרפהא וג̇לאלהא הי אלבקעה̈ אלמכ̇תארה̈ מן סאיר אלעמארה̈ לחלול נור אלשְׁכִינָה אלמעט̇ם פיהא כקולה תעאלי לסיידנא שְׁלֹמֹה עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְעַתָּ֗ה בָּחַ֤רְתִּי וְהִקְדַּ֙שְׁתִּי֙ אֶת־הַבַּ֣יִת הַזֶּ֔ה לִֽהְיוֹת־שְׁמִ֥י שָׁ֖ם עַד־עוֹלָ֑ם וְהָי֨וּ עֵינַ֧י וְלִבִּ֛י שָׁ֖ם כׇּל־הַיָּמִֽים׃ ((דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב ז׃טז)) והי אלמפרוץ̇ עלינא אלתוג̇ה באלצלאה̈ אליהא ובאלתעבדאת באלד̇באיח ואלכ̇תאנה̈ נחוהא ואליהא חתי אן מותאנא נסתקבלהם בהא פוק אלארץ̇ ותחתהא והי אלמקול ענהא לְשִׁכְנ֥וֹ תִדְרְשׁ֖וּ וּבָ֥אתָ שָּֽׁמָּה׃ ((דְּבָרִים יב׃ה)) והי אלד̇י תעוד אליהא סאיר אלשעוב תצלי כקול עז מן קאל כִּ֣י בֵיתִ֔י בֵּית־תְּפִלָּ֥ה יִקָּרֵ֖א לְכָל־הָעַמִּֽים׃ ((יְשַׁעְיָהוּ נו׃ז))
content.english:
Belief in the [Holy] Site (Qibla)

One must believe that the sacred, noble, and venerated site (qibla)—may God restore it to its honor, dignity, and majesty—is the place chosen from among all others, so that the venerated light of the Divine Presence (shekhinah) might dwell within it. As He (may He be exalted) proclaimed to Solomon (peace be upon him), Now I have chosen and consecrated this House that My name be there forever. My eyes and my heart shall always be there (2 Chronicles 7:16). It is our duty to orient ourselves toward that place in prayer, facing it during worshipful acts [such as] slaughtering and circumcision. We orient even our deceased toward it, both when they are above the ground and beneath it. This is the place of which it is said, Even unto His habitation shall you seek, and there you are to go (Deuteronomy 12:5). This is the place to which all the nations will come to pray, as He said (glory be to Him), For My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isaiah 56:7).
content.comments: [3] The term qibla means “direction” and refers to the direction properly faced during prayer (and, according to our author, other devotional acts). There is no accurate English translation that comfortably fits this context.

content.hebrew: אלעקידה̈ אלסאדסה̈
content.english: The Sixth Tenet

content.hebrew:
אעתקאד יום אלדין

הו אן יעתקד אן אלמיעאד לא בד מנה והו אעאדה̈ אלמותי עלי מא כאנו עליה מן אלחיאה̈ בעוד ארואחהם אליהם ונשרהם מן קבורהם אלי סטח אלארץ̇ ועוד אלאג̇סאם אלי מא כאנו עליה אולא ולו מן קעור אלבחר ומן דאכ̇ל אלמגאייר ואלאודיה̈ אלמט̇למה̈ כמא קאל אָמַ֣ר אֲ֭דֹנָי מִבָּשָׁ֣ן אָשִׁ֑יב אָ֝שִׁ֗יב מִֽמְּצֻל֥וֹת יָֽם׃ ((תְּהִלִּים סח׃כג)) ואיצאל כל מנהם אלי מסתחקה ג̇מלה̈ כ̇אפיה̈ עלי מה פעלה מן טאעה̈ או מעציה̈ ונשר אעמאלה בין ידיה ומחאסבתה עלי אלסרה ואלצ̇רה לה ועליה פמן כאן עמלה צאלח נקל אלי דאר אלנעים לינאל מא תשתהיה אלנפוס מן אלפוז אלעט̇ים מקרונא באג̇לאל ואכראם גיר מנקטע עלי אלדואם ואלויל ואלעויל למן כאן עמלה גיר צאלח נקל אלי דאר אלעקאב אלי אלד̇ל ואלאסכ̇אף וטול אלעד̇אב וינאל מן אלמכארה ואלאלאם מא לא יסתטאע לאבד אלאבדין בלא אנקטאע כקולה ען אלרְשָׁעִים כִּ֣י תוֹלַעְתָּ֞ם לֹ֣א תָמ֗וּת וְאִשָּׁם֙ לֹ֣א תִכְבֶּ֔ה וְהָי֥וּ דֵרָא֖וֹן לְכָל־בָּשָֽׂר׃ ((יְשַׁעְיָהוּ סו׃כד)) וקאל ען אלצַדִּיקִים וְשַׁבְתֶּם֙ וּרְאִיתֶ֔ם בֵּ֥ין צַדִּ֖יק לְרָשָׁ֑ע בֵּ֚ין עֹבֵ֣ד אֱלֹהִ֔ים לַאֲשֶׁ֖ר לֹ֥א עֲבָדֽוֹ׃ ((מַלְאָכִי ג׃יח)) פנסאלה סבחאנה ותעאלי אלעפו ואלעאפיה̈ ואלרחמה̈ ואלמגפרה̈ ואלסלאמה̈ פי אלדניא ואלאכ̇רה̈ אמין וְשָׁלוֹם׃

תמת אלעקאיד אלסתה̈ וְשָׁלוֹם

בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְהֹוָ֖ה אֵ֥ל עוֹלָֽם יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֺ
content.english:
Belief in the Day of Judgment

This means that one must believe that the Appointed Time is inevitable. This is when the dead will be restored to their former living state, as their souls are returned to them, and they are resurrected from their graves and returned to the face of the Earth, and their bodies are restored to their former state—whether from the bottom of the sea, or from caves and dark valleys, just as The Lord said, `I will retrieve from Bashan, I will retrieve from the depths of the sea…' (Psalms 68:23). [It is the time at which] each and every one of them will receive their just deserts, altogether, [for acts committed] in secret, for all of one's obedient and rebellious deeds. All of one's actions are unfurled in God's presence, the good weighed against the bad. Those whose deeds are righteous shall be transported to the abode of bliss, and shall be granted the great triumph that souls desire, in unceasing and perpetual conjunction with splendor and glory.

But woe to the those whose deeds are unrighteous, who shall be taken to the abode of punishment, to humiliation and feebleness, and long-lasting suffering. There they shall be consigned unbearable misery and suffering that cannot be borne for all of eternity, without respite. As He said concerning the wicked, Their worms shall not die, nor their fire be quenched; they shall be a horror to all flesh (Isaiah 66:24). But of the righteous He said, You shall come to see the difference between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve Him (Malachi 3:18).

Therefore, we ask God for forgiveness, health, compassion, atonement, and well-being in this world and in the Hereafter.

Amen, and Peace. Here end the Six Tenets. Peace.

In the name of the Lord, God of the World (Gen. 21:33),

blessed be His name.
content.comments:
[4] This translation follows our edition, based on MSS JTSb and BL, which read al-mīʿād (from the root w-ʿ-d). JTSa and BLb read al-maʿād (the Return; from the root ʿ-w-d). Both expressions are widely attested in medieval Arabic literature across schools and genres.

[5] The sense here seems to be that divine judgment takes into account the full range of hidden merit and guilt; according to this reading, connecting the lexeme to the following phrase, it could be read khāfiya. So reads the Arabic version. Alternatively, one could connect the term to the preceding phrase: jumlatan kāfiyatan, “altogether, sufficiently (i.e., fully).” Cf. Halkin, “A Karaite Creed,” 153: “entirely and summarily.” The two possible readings rest on a single diacritic, which is rarely provided in the MSS.

[6] In its Biblical context, “eternal God” would be a better translation. Our translation of al-Maghribī's usage here more closely reflects Maimonides' understanding of this verse. The latter's usage of this citation as a preface for his works echoes the Islamic basmala (pace Joseph Qafiḥ, for whose discussion see Moreh ha-nebukhim [Mossad Harav Kook: 1977], 3 n. 4). Qafiḥ notes that in employing this formulation, Maimonides expresses his identification with Abraham, the messenger of monotheism in an idolatrous world. In the period following Maimonides, this became a very standard opening in medieval Hebrew and Judaeo-Arabic works. For Maimonides' usage and interpretation of this verse, see Guide of the Perplexed (trans. Shlomo Pines; Chicago: 1963), 3 and n. 1 (introductory epistle), 282 and n. 4 (II.13), 516 (III.29); and cf. Mishneh Torah, Laws of Idolatry and Gentile Norms, 1:3. Saul Lieberman noted that Maimonides prefaces all of his works with this formulation (see Hilkhoth Ha-Yerushalmi (The Laws of the Palestinian Talmud) of Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, ed. Saul Lieberman [The Jewish Theological Seminary of America: 1995], 5, n. 7). Of course, the fact that Maimonides' usage of Gen. 21:33 echoes the basmala does not in the least negate Qafiḥ's insightful observation concerning the significance of this usage.

content.hebrew: שרוט אלד̇באחה̈ לְמָרֵינוּ וְרַבֵּינוּ הֶחָכָם הַגָּדוֹל בְּעַם הָאֵל כְּבוֹד הָרַב יִשְׂרָאֵל הַדַּיָּן אלמשאר אליה ואלמצדר בד̇כרה נוּחוֹ עֵדֶן תְּהִי נַפְשׁוֹ צְרוּרָ֣ה ׀ בִּצְר֣וֹר הַחַיִּ֗ים ((שְׁמוּאֵל א כה׃כט)) אָמֵן נֶצַח סֶלָה וְשָׁלוֹם׃
content.english: The Regulations of Slaughter by our master and teacher, the sage, great among God's people, the honorable R. Israel the Judge, indicated and mentioned above, may he rest in Eden, [and] may his soul be bound up in the bond of life (1 Samuel 25:29). Amen, Neṣaḥ, Selah, and Peace.

content.hebrew: אלכלאם עלי אלד̇באחה̈
content.english: Discourse on Slaughter

content.hebrew: פי אשיא מנהא שרוט אלד̇אבח ואלמד̇בוח ואלאלה̈ וכיף יפעל בהא ומוצ̇ע אלד̇בח ומא יקטע ומא לא יקטע וכיף יצ̇בט ואלברכה̈ ופי מא יג̇ב בעד אלד̇בח אלג̇מלה̈ עשרה̈ אקסאם׃
content.english: Among its subjects are (i) regulations of the slaughterer, (ii) the slaughtered [animal], (iii) the instrument, (iv) how [the instrument] must be used, (v) the site of slaughtering, (vi) what must be cut, (vii) what must not be cut, (viii) how [the animal] should be handled, (ix) the blessing [to be recited], and (x) what must be done following slaughter. In total, it comes to ten chapters.

content.hebrew: אלקסם אלאול
content.english: Chapter I

content.hebrew:
שרוט אלד̇אבח

יג̇ב אן יכון אלד̇אבח באלג עאקל ראשד קוי אלנפס בציר מתמד̇הב בשריעת אֲדוֹנֵינוּ מֹשֶׁה אַב כָּל הַנְּבִיאִים עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מן גיר תסתר נאכרא לעקל ינאקצ̇הא חסן אלסירה̈ מלאזם אלצלאואת קליל אלחלף ואלהזל צחיח אלמעאמלה̈ דיין כ̇ייר מעתקד בתעויץ̇ אלחיואן אלמד̇בוח ואן לם יעלם במא ד̇א עארפה בחלאלה וחראמה ובשרוט מא בה יחל אכלה׃
content.english:
Regulations of the Slaughterer

The slaughterer must be an intelligent and reasonable adult, strong-spirited and insightful; who openly follows the Law of Moses, father of all of the prophets, peace be upon him, and who repudiates any opinion that is incompatible with it; a person of good conduct, who regularly performs prayers; who rarely makes oaths or jests; who is dependable and honest in interpersonal conduct; who is pious and virtuous; who believes that there is recompense for the slaughtered animal, even though he does not know what it is; who is knowledgeable in what is permitted and what is forbidden, and in the regulations that render eating the animal permissible.
content.comments: [7] The term baṣīr may denote either mental insight or physical sight.

content.hebrew: אלקסם אלת̇אני
content.english: Chapter II

content.hebrew:
שרוט אלמד̇בוח

אלד̇י יג̇וז ד̇בחה מן אלחיואן יג̇ב אן יכון אד̇א כאן מן אלבהאים ברי או אהלי מט̇לף או מפסוך̇ אלצ̇לף יג̇תר ואן לא יד̇בח ענד אליהוד פי ד̇אלך אליום אמה וולדהא ואן עארף לה אב כד̇אלך ויכון עמר אלמד̇בוח אכת̇ר מן סבעה̈ איאם ויכון גיר משכוך לא חאמל ולא מריץ̇ ולא ג̇ריח ולא מפתרס יכ̇שא קרב פואת רוחה ואן כאן מן אלטאיר יג̇ב אן יכון ממא לא כ̇לף פיה בין אליהוד פי חלה ופי אבאחתה ושהרה בינהם והום מתנאקלינהם מן גיר תקייד בעלאמה כאלחמאם ואלימאם ואלדג̇אג̇ ואלאוז ואלחג̇ל ואלסמאן ואלסלוי וכל חיואן אן שכך פי אמרה פי אלעלאמאת אן כאן מן אלבהאים ופי אלנקל אן כאן מן אלטאיר לא יג̇וז ד̇בחה ולתזם פי אלטאיר ד̇בח אלצחיח איצ̇א כאלבהאים׃
content.english:
Regulations of [the Animal That Is to Be] Slaughtered

If it is a wild or domesticated [land] animal, it must have split hooves and chew its cud. According to Jewish opinion, a mother and its young may not be slaughtered on the same day; if its father is known, the same rule applies. The [animal to be] slaughtered must be over seven days old, and there must not be any doubt; it cannot be pregnant, sick, injured, or attacked by a predator; and there should be no [reason to] fear that it is near to its death.

If it is a bird, there must be an undisputed tradition among the Jews regarding its acceptability, permissibility, and identification; they must be in possession of a sound tradition, excluding the inspection of its characteristics. [Such permitted species] include doves, pigeons, chickens, geese, partridges, wild quail, and common quail.

If there is a doubt regarding any animal's status—in the characteristics for a land animal, or in the tradition for a bird—it may not be slaughtered.

As with [land] animals, only birds that are of sound body may be slaughtered.

content.hebrew: אלקסם אלת̇אלת̇
content.english: Chapter III

content.hebrew:
שרוט אלאלה̈

יג̇ב אן תכון אלאלה̈ אלד̇י יד̇בח בהא אטול מן ערץ̇ רקבה̈ אלחיואן חתי אד̇א ג̇ר בהא לא ידכ̇ל ראסהא פי וסט אלד̇בח ללא תנכ̇ס פי וקת אלרד בהא עלי אלג̇לד ויכון להא ערץ̇ ות̇כ̇ן חתי לא תנת̇ני ותצ̇טרב חתי יד̇בח בהא ולא יכון פיהא אעוג̇אג̇ ולא ת̇לם ולא חרושה̈ ג̇אריה̈ עלי כ̇ט מסתקים מאצ̇יה̈ חאדה̈ פי גאיה̈ מה יכון ולא תכון זג̇אג̇ ולא כ̇זף ולא כ̇שב ולא עט̇ם ולא קצב ולא ט̇פר לאן האד̇ה אלאשיא לא יאמן תפתית בעצ̇הא ותת̇לימהא ענד אלג̇ר בהא עלי אלג̇לד ואנהא תכון חדיד חתי יכון אלד̇בח מאמון בהא לאן אלחדיד אקוי מן אולאיך אלמד̇כוראת׃
content.english:
Regulations of the Instrument

The instrument used for the act of slaughter must be longer than the width of the animal's neck, so that its head will not enter [into the animal's neck] when it is drawn [along it], nor stick [into the animal's neck] when brought back over the [animal's] skin. It should have enough thickness and solidity that it will not bend or quiver, so it can be used for slaughtering. It should not have any curvature, nicks, or coarseness; it must follow a straight line, cut deeply, and be as sharp as possible. It may not be [made from] glass, ceramic, wood, bone, reed, or a claw, for one cannot be sure that they will not break or blunt when drawn over the [animal's] skin. [The instrument] should be made from iron so that the slaughtering process will be reliable, because iron is stronger than the aforementioned materials.
content.comments: [8] It seems that the version attested in JTSb and BLb reflects an erroneous reading of thikhan (without diacritic: תכן) as takūn (תכון).

content.hebrew: אלקסם אלראבע
content.english: Chapter IV

content.hebrew:
כיף יפעל בהא חתי אראד אלד̇אבח יד̇בח

יג̇ר בהא עלי אלענק מן תחת אלכ̇רזה̈ אלכבירה̈ סאירא וג̇אי בחדהא מן גיר נחרא ולא נכ̇סא לאן כד̇לך יזדאד אלם אלחיואן אלמד̇בוח ולא יכון אלד̇בח קדא ולא כבסא לאן אלד̇בח עלי הד̇א אלצפה̈ לא יתמכן אלד̇אבח בחצולהא ויכון עמלה בהא עלי אלמוצ̇ע עמל מתראדף לא בבטו פיה ולא רפע יד ולא תראכ̇י ולא פי איסר זמאן לאן כל חרכה̈ תציר ד̇באחה̈ ת̇אניא אד̇א כאנת עקיב אלבטו ורפע אליד ויג̇ב אן יבתדי באלקטע מן וגה אלענק ויודג̇ אלג̇אנבין׃
content.english:
How the Slaughterer Must Use [the Instrument]

When He Wants to Slaughter

One must draw the blade over the neck underneath the cricoid cartilage, back and forth with its sharp edge without stabbing or prodding, for such things increase the pain of the slaughtered animal. One should not chop or press, because the slaughterer cannot retain full control in such a fashion. The motion should be continuous, without slowing, without lifting the hand, and without even momentary weakness, for any such motion due to slowing or lifting one's hand would constitute a second act of slaughter. One must first cut the most anterior part of the neck and then the jugular veins on either side.
content.comments: [9] Despite the fact that JTSb presents the more difficult reading (lectio difficilior) and appears to be older, we have based our text and translation on the version that appears in BL and BLb. The reading sāʾiran wa-jāʾi (sic) is more plausible on two grounds: The formulation is used elsewhere by the same author (see the second tenet of al-Maghribī's creed); and it is arguably cognate with the rabbinic terms holakhah and habaʾah, for which cf. Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Ritual Slaughter, 3:11. This Hebrew terminology is also reflected in Hebrew Karaite works, both medieval and modern: Cf. the formulations ve-yolikh ve-yavi ʿad she-yashlim ha-sheḥiṭah and ve-yolikh ve-yavi ha-sakkin in the eighth chapter of the Hebrew version of al-Maghribī's monograph; Aaron b. Elijah of Nicomedia (fourteenth century), Gan ʿEden, ed. Judah b. Isaac Savuskan (Gözlöw [Eupatoria]: 1864), Ritual Slaughter, 89; and Shemuel Ha-kohen, ʿInyan ha-sheḥiṭah/Ritual Slaughter: A Modern Guide to Karaite Jewish Practice (The Karaite Jews of America: 2017 [republished from 1958 edition]), 18. Cf. Nemoy, “Israel Al-Maghribī's Tract,” 200: “back and forth.” (Nemoy follows the modern Arabic version.)

content.hebrew: אלקסם אלכ̇אמס
content.english: Chapter V

content.hebrew:
פי מוצ̇ע אלד̇בח

והו אלענק מן קדאם לא מן ורא קריב מן אלראס ולא מן בעיד חתי אד̇א ג̇אר אלכ̇נק לא ידורו מעה אלאודאג̇ לאן תמסכהם מן אצולהם לא יעטו רכ̇ו פיתמכן מן קטעהום ועלמנא אן אלזְבִיחָה פי אלענק לאשתראך זְבִיחָה וד̇ביחה̈ פי אללגתין אלערבי ואלעבראני פוג̇דנא לו קאל קאיל ג̇רח פלאן לקאל לה אלסאמע פי אין מן ג̇סמה וכד̇לך לו קאל צ̇רב פלאן לסאל פי אין ואד̇א קאל ד̇בח פלאן עלם באלחקיקה̈ אנא פי אלרקבה̈ פלא סואל יקע פלמא וקע ענדנא פי אלנץ תִּזְבַּ֣ח ׀ וְאָכַלְתָּ֣ בָשָׂ֗ר ((דְּבָרִים יב׃טו)) וְזָבַחְתָּ֞ מִבְּקָרְךָ֣ וּמִצֹּֽאנְךָ֗ ((דְּבָרִים יב׃כא)) עלמנא חקיקה̈ אנה פי אלענק׃
content.english:
On the Site of Slaughtering

[The location at which the throat is to be cut] is at the front rather than the back of the neck, and close to the head rather than far from it, so that if one grabs the throat, the jugular veins will not rotate with it; for when one grips them from their point of origin they are not slack, enabling one to cut them. We know that “slaughtering” (dhabīḥa) is [a term that refers specifically to cutting] of the neck, for the Hebrew and Arabic terms are cognate: zeviḥah [in Hebrew] and dhabīḥa [in Arabic]. If one were to say, “So-and-so has been wounded,” the listener would reply, “Where on his body?” Similarly, if one were to say, “So-and-so has been hit,” the listener would reply, “Where?” But if one were to say, “So-and-so has been slaughtered (dhubiḥa),” this plainly refers to the neck, without any further question. Therefore, when the verse states, You may slaughter (tizbaḥ) and eat meat (Deuteronomy 12:15), and, You shall slaughter (ve-zavaḥta) any of your cattle or sheep (ibid., 12:21), we know with certainty that this refers to the neck.
content.comments: [10] Reading the Judaeo-Arabic jāra with the Arabic version as jarra, and understanding the term כ̇נק as a variant of the makhnaq (throat). Although ʿunq (as in the Arabic version) is a more common term, (a) the Judaeo-Arabic provides the lectio difficilior, and (b) the term ʿunq refers either to the neck as a whole or to the nape or back of the neck, which makes less sense in this context.

content.hebrew: אלקסם אלסאדס
content.english: Chapter VI

content.hebrew:
פי מא יקטע

אלד̇י יג̇ב קטעה מן אלחיואן פי אלענק הו אלמרי והו ללגד̇א ואלחלקום והו ללתנפס ואלורידין והמא מעדן אלדם פבקטעהם יכון אלד̇בח צחיח ענד כל אליהוד וכד̇לך אד̇א קטע מן כל ואחד מנהם מא יקום מקאם אלכל וליס יסמא בד̇בח ענד כלהם מא בקי פיה ואחד מן אלורידין והד̇א אחד חג̇ג̇נא ומהמא קטע מן אלג̇לד ואלחם ואלשראיין פי חאל אלד̇בח לא יפסד אלמד̇בוח בה לאן לא וצול אלי קטע מא יג̇ב קטעה אלא בהמא פאלצ̇רורה̈ תורי אלי קטעהמא פבקטע מא ד̇כרנאה יכון פואת רוחה וכ̇רוג̇ דמה אסרע ממא לו קטע פי גירה׃
content.english:
On What Must Be Cut

These are what must be cut in the neck of an animal: the esophagus (for food), the trachea (for breathing), and the two jugular veins (the locus of the blood). By cutting these, slaughter is regarded as valid by all Jews. The same is true if any one of them is partially, rather than fully, severed (?). However, as long as one of the jugular veins remains [intact], none consider this to be [valid] slaughter. This is one of our [Karaite?] arguments. Whatever skin, flesh, or veins are cut during slaughtering do not invalidate the animal, because what must be cut can only be accessed through them; necessity thus dictates that they must be cut. By cutting the aforementioned [parts of the throat, the animal] dies and bleeds out faster than if one cut anything else.
content.comments: [11] Cf. Nemoy, “Israel Al-Maghribi's Tract,” 201.

content.hebrew: אלקסם אלסאבע
content.english: Chapter VII

content.hebrew:
פי מא לא יקטע

יג̇ב אן יחתרז אלד̇אבח פי וקת ג̇רה באלסכין חתי לא יכסר עט̇ם או יסתגרק אלנכ̇אע פי קטעה ורב מא יכ̇לץ אלראס ג̇מלה̈ פי עדם אלחס מן ג̇סם אלחיואן פלא יתכ̇בט פיבקי דמה פיה פיציר חראם לאן עלינא אלתחרז מן אלדם לא נאכלה ודם אלד̇באחה̈ אד̇א לם יכ̇רג̇ פי חאל תכ̇ביט אלחיואן לם יכ̇רג̇ה אלמלח ואלדליל עלי ד̇לך לחם אלרקבה̈ לאנג̇ראר אלדם עליהא פי וקת אלד̇בח לם ינקי במלח ואלנץ יקול כִּ֥י הַדָּ֖ם ה֣וּא הַנָּ֑פֶשׁ וְלֹא־תֹאכַ֥ל הַנֶּ֖פֶשׁ עִם־הַבָּשָֽׂר׃ ((דְּבָרִים יב׃כג))
content.english:
On What Must Not Be Cut

While he draws the knife [along the animal's throat], the slaughterer must be careful not to break any bone or to cut so deeply that he reaches the spinal marrow; indeed, not paying attention, one might sever the head from the animal's body. It would then not convulse, its blood would remain within it, and it would be rendered impermissible (ḥarām). For we must be punctilious in refraining from the consumption of blood. If the blood from slaughtering does not pour out while the animal is convulsing, salting [the meat] will not extract it. The proof of this is that the meat of the neck cannot be cleansed by salting, due to the blood spilled over it while [the animal is being] slaughtered. As the verse states, For the blood is the life, and you must not consume the life with the flesh (Deuteronomy 12:23).

content.hebrew: אלקסם אלת̇אמן
content.english: Chapter VIII

content.hebrew:
כיף יצ̇בט אלחיואן אלמד̇בוח

יג̇ב אן יכון אלצ̇אבט ללבהימה̈ גיר אלד̇אבח כברת או צגרת וירמי אלד̇אבח ידה עלי אלענק אלמד̇בוח וירד אלכ̇רזה̈ אלכבירה̈ אלי מא ילי אלראס ויכ̇נק קדאמה באלבהאם ואלד̇י יליה ומא בינהמא וינזל ויד̇בח ויכון מסתקבל באלמד̇בוח אלי אלקבלה̈ אלקדוסיה̈ תמת̇יל באלד̇באיח אלמקרבה̈ כמא קאל וְשָׁחַ֨ט אֹת֜וֹ עַ֣ל יֶ֧רֶךְ הַמִּזְבֵּ֛חַ צָפֹ֖נָה לִפְנֵ֣י יְהֹוָ֑ה ((וַיִּקְרָא א׃יא)) פאן כאן מן אלטאיר יצ̇בט אג̇נחתה בידה וירפע רג̇לה בין אצאבעה אלכ̇נצר ואלד̇י יליה ויג̇על צדרה לפוק יציר ט̇הרה פוק וג̇ה יד אלד̇אבח פיג̇ד̇ב ראסה ויחט אצאבעה פי ענקה ויכ̇רג̇ לסאנה ויכ̇נקה באלג̇לד חתי לא יבלע פיג̇י אלד̇בח פי אלסאן(!) או פי אלכ̇רזה̈ אלכבירה̈ פיחרם ואן כאן אלטאיר כביר יחט אג̇נחתה תחת רג̇ל אלד̇אבח ויתמכן ויד̇בח פאן אחתאג̇ת אלבהימה̈ תקייד פי וקת אלצ̇בט לשדה̈ קותהא פתתקייד ולא תכ̇לא ותותרך מרבוטה̈ אלי חין יכמל אלד̇בח ותחל בעד ד̇לך חתי אן לא ימתנע אלחיואן מן אלתכ̇ביט פלא יכ̇רג̇ דמה׃
content.english:
How the Animal That Is to Be Slaughtered Should Be Restrained

The person restraining the animal should be somebody other than the slaughterer, whether it is large or small. The slaughterer should position his hand on the neck that is to be cut, push the cricoid cartilage rostrally, grip the animal's throat and the adjacent part in the front, and reach under and cut the throat. One should face in the direction of the sacred site (al-qibla al-quddūsiyya) [i.e., Jerusalem], representing the sacrifices that were offered [in the Temple]. As it is stated, He shall slaughter it on the north side of the altar, before the Lord (Leviticus 1:11).

If it is a bird, one should hold its wings in one hand, lift its legs between his fingers (namely, the little finger and the adjacent one), and hold its breast upright so that its back lies on the slaughterer's palm. One should then pull its head, place one's fingers on its neck so that it sticks out its tongue, and then grip the throat by the skin so that it cannot swallow (lest the tongue or cricoid cartilage be cut, which would render it impermissible). If it is a large bird, then the slaughterer should place its wings under his legs. He may then position himself, and cut the throat.

If, due to its strength, an animal must be bound while it is handled, then let it be bound; and let it not be freed, and let it remain bound, until the slaughter is completed. But afterwards, it should be untied so that the animal might not be prevented from convulsing, which would prevent the blood from pouring out.

content.hebrew: אלקסם אלתאסע
content.english: Chapter IX

content.hebrew:
פי אלברכה̈

יג̇ב אן נקדם ד̇כר רבנא עלי כל אעמאלנא ולא נתצרף פי שי ממא אחסן אללה תעאלי עלינא בה חתי נשכרה כמא קאל אלסייד שְׁלֹמֹה עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּכָל־דְּרָכֶ֥יךָ דָעֵ֑הוּ וְ֝ה֗וּא יְיַשֵּׁ֥ר אֹֽרְחֹתֶֽיךָ׃ ((מִשְׁלֵי ג׃ו)) וד̇לך אנה אוג̇דנא מן אלעדם ואנעם עלינא ומלכנא עלי כל אלמוג̇ודאת ואבאח לנא אלתצרף פי כל מא נצל אליה מן אלעאלם אלספלי כמא קאל אלסייד דָּוִד עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם תַּ֭מְשִׁילֵהוּ בְּמַעֲשֵׂ֣י יָדֶ֑יךָ כֹּ֗֝ל שַׁ֣תָּה תַֽחַת־רַגְלָֽיו׃ ((תְּהִלִּים ח׃ז)) צֹנֶ֣ה וַאֲלָפִ֣ים כֻּלָּ֑ם ((תְּהִלִּים ח׃ח)) וְגוֺמֵר צִפּ֣וֹר שָׁ֭מַיִם וּדְגֵ֣י הַיָּ֑ם ((תְּהִלִּים ח׃ט)) וְגוֹמֵר פיג̇ב עלינא אן נשכרה עלי אבאחתה לנא כל מא נעלם בה צלאח דיננא ודניאנא פענדמא נתקדם עלי אלד̇באחה̈ מא נד̇בחה מן אלחיואן נבארך בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה יוי אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם שֶׁהִתִּיר לָנוּ שְׁחִיטַת בְּהֵמָה טְהוֹרָה אן כאנת מן אלבהאים ונזיד בע֥וֹף טָה֖וֹר ((דְּבָרִים יד׃כ)) אן כאן מן אלטאיר ונד̇בח >ואן סהי אלד̇אבח יבארך פלא צ̇רר יעוד עלי אלמד̇בוח פי ד̇לך וכד̇לך (אד̇א)< (ואן) סהי איצ̇א ען אלקבלה̈ פלא יות̇ר ד̇לך פי אלמד̇בוח ותגני ברכה̈ ואחדה̈ עלי אלף אלף מד̇בוח אד̇א כאן ד̇באחתהמא מתצלה̈ ואן אפצל ועאוד לא בד מן ברכה̈ ת̇אניה̈׃
content.english:
On the Blessing

We should preface all of our actions by mentioning our Lord, and we should not make use of anything that God (may He be exalted) has bestowed upon us until we have offered thanks to Him. As Solomon (peace be upon him) said, In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths smooth (Proverbs 3:6). For He brought us into existence out of nothing, dealt favorably with us, appointed us as rulers over all creatures, and permitted us to make use of whatever we can in the temporal realm. As David (peace be upon him) said, You have made him master over Your handiwork, laying the world at his feet, sheep and oxen, all of them… the birds of the heavens, the fish of the sea… (Psalms 8:7–9).

And so, we should thank Him for the permission that He has given us to make use of anything that we know to be proper from the perspective of both our religious and worldly existence. Thus, whenever we approach the act of slaughtering any animal, we make the blessing, “Blessed are You, Lord our God, the King of the Universe, Who permitted us to slaughter pure animals”—that is for a species of [land] animal. For a bird, we conclude it with [the expression] “pure birds.” We may then slaughter it. <If the slaughterer neglects to make the blessing, no harm is done; let him return to the slaughtered animal [to recite it]. Similarly,> if the slaughterer neglects [to face the sacred] site (qibla) [i.e., Jerusalem], this does not have any effect on [the permissibility of] the animal. A single blessing is sufficient for even a million animals, as long as they are slaughtered consecutively. However, if the slaughterer makes an interruption and then returns, he must recite a second blessing.

content.hebrew: אלקסם אלעאשר
content.english: Chapter X

content.hebrew:
פי מא יג̇ב בעד אלד̇בח

יג̇ב עלי כל בַּר יִשְׂרָאֵל אן לא יזיד עלי אלחיואן אלם גיר אלם אלד̇באחה̈ ולאג̇ל הד̇א אחתרזנא כמא ראינא מן אלתהוין עלי אלחיואן פי נפס אלד̇בח כמא ראינא מן שפקה̈ רבנא ג̇ל ג̇לאלה כמא קאל אלסייד דָּוִד עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְ֝רַחֲמָ֗יו עַל־כׇּל־מַעֲשָֽׂיו׃ ((תְּהִלִּים קמה׃ט)) וראינא יקול לֹא־תִקַּ֥ח הָאֵ֖ם עַל־הַבָּנִֽים׃ ((דְּבָרִים כב׃ו)) ואיצ̇א אֹת֣וֹ וְאֶת־בְּנ֔וֹ לֹ֥א תִשְׁחֲט֖וּ בְּי֥וֹם אֶחָֽד׃ ((וַיִּקְרָא כב׃כח)) וקאל איצ̇א לֹֽא־תְבַשֵּׁ֥ל גְּדִ֖י בַּחֲלֵ֥ב אִמּֽוֹ׃ ((דְּבָרִים יד׃כא)) פסלכנא פי טרק רבנא פאשתרטנא אן יכון אלד̇אבח מומן ליכון פי קלבה שפקה̈ אלאימאן פלא יקסא ענד אלד̇בח פי קטע מא לא חאג̇ה̈ אליהא וכל מא שרט פי אלמד̇בוח עלי סביל אלשפקה̈ לאן אן ד̇בח מן גיר אלחלאל כאן עבת̇ אד̇א ליס לנא בה נפע ואן כאן מריץ̇ או ג̇ריח לא יזדאד אלם עלי אלמה ואֹת֣וֹ וְאֶת־בְּנ֔וֹ ((וַיִּקְרָא כב׃כח)) ואלחאמל יציר אֹת֣וֹ וְאֶת־בְּנ֔וֹ ((וַיִּקְרָא כב׃כח)) ואיצ̇א כמא אחתרזנא פי אמר אלאלה̈ ואלג̇ר ואלקטע כל ד̇לך ללשפקה̈ פיג̇ב עלינא איצ̇א אן אד̇א וקע אלפעל אלד̇י יג̇וז בוקועה אכל אללחם פכאן מא זאד עליה קסאוה̈ פי חאל בקא רוח אלמד̇בוח מתשבת̇ה̈ בה פאד̇א פאתה בקי תצרפנא פיה כתצרפנא פי אלג̇מאד ואלנבאת עלי מעני אלתבצ̇יע יג̇ב עלינא ד̇לך פי כל מד̇בוח אן לא נתצרף פיה חתי תבטל אלחרכה̈ מנה ויבקי עלינא פי אלטאיר וצֵ֥יד חַיָּ֛ה ((וַיִּקְרָא יז׃יג)) תגטיה̈ דמהמא באלתראב אלחקיקי לא אלמג̇אזי מן כל אלג̇האת יד̇בח אלא פי אלתראב ויבארך עלי תגטיתה בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה יוי אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֺתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ עַל כִּסּוּי הַדָּם בְּעָפָר ומא כאן אמרה משתבה מן אלבהאים הל הו ברי או אהלי יגטי דמה אד̇א ד̇בח ויחרם שחמה ומא נסי תגטיה̈ דמה לא יחרם ומא ד̇בח אֹת֣וֹ וְאֶת־בְּנ֔וֹ ((וַיִּקְרָא כב׃כח)) עלי סביל אלסהו לא יחרם אלא אנא יחרם טבכ̇המא ג̇מיעא קיאסא עלי לֹֽא־תְבַשֵּׁ֥ל גְּדִ֖י בַּחֲלֵ֥ב אִמּֽוֹ׃ ((דְּבָרִים יד׃כא))

תמת אלעשרה̈ אקסאם וְשָׁלוֹם עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל

בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְהֹוָ֖ה אֵ֥ל עוֹלָֽם יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֺ
content.english:
On What Must Be Done After Slaughter

It is incumbent upon every Israelite not to increase the suffering of the animal beyond the suffering endured during slaughter. To this end, as we have seen, we are careful not to demean the animal during the act of slaughter itself, having observed the compassion of our Lord (may His majesty be exalted!). As David (peace be upon him) stated, His mercy is upon all His works (Psalms 145:9); and we see that it is stated, You shall not take the mother together with her young (Deuteronomy 22:6); and also, You shall not slaughter it with its young on the same day (Leviticus 22:28); and also, You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk (Exodus 23:19).

We thus walk in the ways of our Lord, and we stipulate that the slaughterer must be a believer, so that the compassion of faith will be in his heart, and so that he will not act cruelly by making any unnecessary cut during the slaughter. Everything prescribed concerning the animal to be slaughtered is for the sake of compassion. For any non-permitted slaughter would be a waste and an offense, since we would be unable to benefit from it. Similarly, if the animal is sick or injured, we should not add further suffering [based on the principle], it with its young (Leviticus 22:28). A pregnant animal is also considered “it with its young.” Moreover, [this principle is related to the other laws of slaughter], just as we are punctilious concerning the instrument, the cutting motion, and the cut—all for the sake of compassion. If the process that renders the consumption of meat permissible has taken place, [this means that] the slaughterer has not been excessively harsh as long as the animal's spirit clings to its body. If all of this comes to pass, it only remains to us to use [the animal], just as we use minerals and plants, in terms of dividing it up. We must not make use of any slaughtered animal until it has stopped moving.

In the case of birds and hunted animals (Leviticus 17:13), we must cover their blood with earth—real and not figurative [earth]—all over. One should only slaughter if one has earth. While covering [the blood], one should recite the blessing: “Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the Universe, Who has sanctified us with His commandments, and commanded us concerning covering the blood with earth.” If it is unclear whether a [land] animal is domesticated or wild, its blood must be covered with earth when it is slaughtered. Its fat is forbidden.

If one forgets to cover [an animal's] blood, [the meat] is not forbidden [for consumption]. If one inadvertently slaughters it with its young (Leviticus 22:28), it is not forbidden. But if they are cooked together, [the meat] is forbidden, by analogy with [the commandment], You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk (Exodus 23:19).

The Ten Chapters are complete. Peace upon all Israel.

In the name of the Lord, God of the World (Gen. 21:33),

blessed be His name.
content.comments:
[12] The Judaeo-Arabic version attested in JTSb and BL appears to be corrupt here, due to a series of scribal errors and emendations (apparently wṣyd > wṣyr > yṣyr > wyṣyr [wa-yaṣīr]; both yod/vav and dalet/resh are easily confused in Hebrew script). Our edition and translation follow BLb and the Arabic-script version, providing the variants in the critical apparatus.

[13] The Judaeo-Arabic text in JTSb and BL is corrupt here and difficult to decipher. On purely textual grounds, our text follows JTSb and BL, presenting as they do the lectio difficilior. Our translation follows BLb, despite the fact that it presents the lectio facilior, as it is at least decipherable.

content.hebrew: אלכלאם פי מפסדאת אלד̇בח
content.english: A Discourse on Factors That Invalidate Slaughter

content.hebrew:
ומפסדאת אלד̇בח כ̇מסה̈ אלאולה שְׁהִיָּה מענאהא אלאבטא מן וְהָאִ֥ישׁ מִשְׁתָּאֵ֖ה לָ֑הּ ((בְּרֵאשִׁית כד׃כא)) ת̇אניא דְּרָסָה ומענאהא אלקד ואלכבס מן אלמוצ̇ע ת̇אלת̇ה̈ הַגְרָמָה הו אלתגלצם ואלתקלים מן לֹ֥א גָרְמ֖וּ לַבֹּֽקֶר׃ ((צְפַנְיָה ג׃ג)) ראבעה̈ חֲלָדָה והי אלכ̇פי מן וְחֶלְדִּ֣י כְאַ֣יִן נֶגְדֶּ֑ךָ ((תְּהִלִּים לט׃ו)) כ̇אמסה̈ עִקּוּר והו אלכ̇לע מן וְעֵ֖ת לַעֲק֥וֹר ((קֹהֶלֶת ג׃ב)) והד̇א אלכ̇מסה̈ הי מנקולה̈ בין ג̇מיע יִשְׂרָאֵל אנהא מפסדה̈ ללד̇בח נקלא מתסלסלא ליס פיה כ̇לף וד̇לך חצל אלאתפאק עלי הד̇א אלכ̇מסה̈ אלפאט̇ אלמד̇כורה̈ ואמא אלתאויל פי כל לפט̇ה ולפט̇ה מן אלמד̇כוראת פאן אלאצח פיה מא הו ג̇ארי עלי אלנט̇ר והו מא ד̇כרוה אלחֲכָמִים עֲלֵיהֶם הַשָּׁלוֹם ואמא תאויל שְׁהִיָּה אלד̇י מענאהא אלאבטא והו אן יכון קד ערץ̇ ללד̇אבח מא ידהשה או מא יעוקה ען תכמיל אלד̇בח פתרתפע ידה באלסכין ען ענק אלחיואן פלא יג̇וז לה אלמעאודה̈ בל יפתקד מא קטע אן כאן כאפיה̈ ואלא אלמד̇בוח חראם ואמא תאויל דְּרָסָה אלד̇י מענאהא אלקד ואלכבס הו אן יכון אלד̇אבח קד חט אלסכין עלי ענק אלמד̇בוח וכבס עליהא בידה כמא תקטע אלאשיא אלג̇אמדה̈ מתל אלג̇בן וגירה או יצ̇רב באלסכין עלי אלענק כמא יצ̇רב אלג̇זאר באלסאטור ליכסר עצ̇ם פהאד̇ין אלפעלין מחרמין ומפסדין ללד̇בח ואמא תאויל חֲלָדָה אלד̇י מענאהא אלאכ̇פא הו אן יערץ̇ ללסכין מא יגטיהא פלא ינט̇ר אלד̇אבח מרורהא עלי אלענק או תכון אלסכין דקיקה̈ אלראס פתסבק ותדכ̇ל תחת אלסִימָנִים או בין אלמרי ואלחלקום פליס הד̇ה ד̇באחה̈ ולא יג̇וז ללד̇אבח אנה יקלב אלסכין ויד̇בח ואמא תאויל הַגְרָמָה אלד̇י מענאהא אלתגלצם ואלתקלים הו אן יכון אלקטע פי אלכ̇רזה̈ אלכבירה̈ או פוקהא וד̇לך יערץ̇ לגפלה̈ אלד̇אבח ען רדהא אלי מא ילי אלראס פיבלע אלמד̇בוח ולא ישער אלד̇אבח פיכ̇נק עלי גיר אלמרי ואלחלקום פיג̇י אלקטע פי גיר אלמקצוד פיחרם וכד̇לך אד̇א קטע עלי אלתקלים ואלוראב פקד יתג̇אוז אלחלקום ויג̇י אלקטע פי אלכ̇רזה̈ אלכבירה̈ או פי מא פוקהא פיחרם אלמד̇בוח פאן לא ד̇בח אלא מא קטע בה אלארבעה̈ סִימָנִים ואמא תאויל עִקּוּר אלד̇י מענאהא אלכ̇לע הו כ̇לע אלסִימָנִים ען מוצ̇עהא קבל אלקטע וד̇לך עלי קסמין אלואחד מן קבל אלד̇אבח ואלאכ̇ר מן קבל אלמד̇בוח פאלד̇י מן קבל אלד̇אבח הו אן יכון קד ג̇ד̇ב אלסִימָנִים בקוה̈ פכ̇לעהום ען מוצ̇עהום ואמא אלד̇י מן ג̇הת אלמד̇בוח הו אן יכון וקת צ̇בטה ללד̇בח קד יצ̇טרב בענקה קצד ללכ̇לאץ פתכ̇לע אלסִימָנִים פעלי אלד̇אבח אלתחרז פי כל מא ד̇כר ופי הד̇א אלאמר איצ̇א באן יעתבר אלחיואן ענד אלד̇בח אן כאן מבלעה סלים אם לא כמא אן עליה אלתחרז פי אפתקאדה קבל אלד̇בח הל פיה אפה̈ או מא יג̇רי מג̇רארהא ממא ימנעה אלד̇בח וכד̇לך עליה אלתחרז פי אמר אלאלה̈ פי אפתקאדהא קבל אלד̇בח ובעד אן יד̇בח בהא אשכ̇אצא ותכון ד̇באחה̈ צחיחה̈ לאנה לא יאמן אן יכון חצל פיהא ת̇לם או וקוף מא ולא יג̇וז ללד̇אבח אן יד̇בח מד̇בוח ת̇אני קבל אפתקאד אלאול ללא יכון קד אנפסדת ד̇באחתה פלא יג̇וז לה אן יד̇בח באלסכין אלד̇י ד̇בח בהא אלא בעד אן יגסלהא עלי אלאקל מן שאן תנט̇ף מן דם אלטְרֵיפָה ולא יתלף אלמד̇בוח אלת̇אני וכל הד̇ה ראג̇ע לאמאנה̈ אלד̇אבח פאן אתקא אללה תעאלי כ̇לץ מן אלדרך פי אלדארין לאנה מתקלד בגירה אלואת̇ק בה אנה לא יטעמה שי חראם פעליה אלאג̇תהאד פי אלדניא פי כ̇לאץ נפסה לינג̇א מן אלעקאב ואלעד̇אב וינאל אלכ̇יר פי אלדניא ות̇ואב אלאכ̇רה̈ ואלחק סבחאנה ותעאלי יסאעדה ויעינה לאנה אלעאלם בנייתה והו סבחאנה ותעאלי אלמרשד אלי אלצואב יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ וְיִתְעַלֶּה זִכְרוֹ אָמֵן נֶצַח סֶלָה׃

בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְהֹוָ֖ה אֵ֥ל עוֹלָֽם יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֺ
content.english:
There are five things that invalidate an act of slaughter:

1. Shehiyyah, meaning “slowing down”; [this term is derived] from [the Biblical usage], The man stood gazing in wonderment (mishtaʾeh) at her (Genesis 24:21).

2. Derasah, meaning “chopping or pressing” on the site.

3. Hagramah, meaning “cutting the upper throat or lopping”; from, [Her judges are wolves of the steppe,] they break not a bone (garmu) for the morning (Zephaniah 3:3).

4. Ḥaladah, meaning “concealing”; from, [You have made my life just handbreadths long;] if I vanish (ḥeldi), is as nothing in Your sight (Psalms 39:6).

5. ʿIqqur, meaning “tearing”; from, and a time to uproot (laʿaqor) [that which is planted] (Ecclesiastes 3:2).

These five things have been transmitted among all Israelites as a continuous, undisputed tradition, attaining a consensus on these five aforementioned terms. As for the interpretation of each term, the soundest method in [establishing their meaning] is that which conforms to analysis (al-naẓar), as discussed by the Sages (peace be upon them).

Concerning the interpretation of shehiyyah (i.e., slowing down): it is when something startles the slaughterer or hinders him from completing the act of slaughter, so that he lifts his hand with the knife, from the animal's neck. [In such a case, the slaughterer] must not resume [the act]. Rather, he must investigate whether what he has already cut suffices, or whether the animal is forbidden [for consumption].

Concerning the interpretation of derasah (i.e., chopping or pressing): it is when the slaughterer places the knife on the slaughtered [animal's] neck and presses down with his hand as if he were cutting a solid object, such as cheese. Or, if one strikes the neck with the blade, just as a butcher hacks with a cleaver in order to break a bone. These two actions are forbidden and invalidate the slaughter.

Concerning the interpretation of ḥaladah (i.e., concealing): it is when something covers the knife, so that the slaughterer cannot watch it pass over the neck, or when the top of the knife is so narrow that it accidentally slips under the [four] signs (simanim) or between the esophagus and the trachea. This is not considered slaughtering, and the slaughterer is not permitted to turn the blade around and slaughter.

Concerning the interpretation of hagramah (i.e., cutting the upper throat or lopping): it is when the cut is made in the cricoid cartilage or above it. This typically occurs when the slaughterer is careless when pushing [the cartilage] rostrally, and the slaughtered [animal] swallows without the slaughterer noticing, and grips something other than the esophagus and trachea. The cut is then made at the wrong site, and the [animal] becomes forbidden.
